english: for something to become urgent / for a deadline to be right on top of you (lit. 'fire falls on the top of your foot')
usage: 발등에 불 떨어져서 밤새 했어.
It got urgent at the last second, so I pulled an all-nighter.
Casual; 떨어지다 is past here as 떨어져서 ('because it fell')
마감이 코앞이라 이제 발등에 불 떨어졌어요.
The deadline's right there, so now it's crunch time.
Polite; pairs naturally with 코앞 ('right in front')
발등에 불 떨어져야 움직이는 스타일이야.
I only get moving once it's down to the wire.
-아야 = 'only when/once'; describes a procrastinator habit
발등에 불이 떨어졌는데 아직도 시작을 안 했어?
It's crunch time and you still haven't started?
Subject 이/가 often added: 불이 떨어지다
examples: 서류 제출이 내일까지라 발등에 불 떨어졌어.
The documents are due tomorrow, so I'm in a last-minute panic.
내일까지 = 'by tomorrow'; civic/paperwork scramble
발등에 불 떨어지고 나서야 부랴부랴 짐을 쌌어요.
Only when it became urgent did I hurriedly pack.
부랴부랴 = 'in a frantic rush,' a natural partner adverb
다들 발등에 불 떨어진 듯이 회의실로 뛰어갔어.
Everyone ran to the meeting room like it was an emergency.
Real-situation: -ㄴ 듯이 = 'as if'
nuance: Literally 'fire falls on the top of your foot' — when a live ember lands on your foot you jump instantly, so this paints something that has suddenly become so urgent you must drop everything and react now. The near-synonym 코앞이다 ('right in front of your nose') only states that a deadline is close in time; 발등에 불 떨어지다 adds the panic of having to scramble this second, which is why it so often pairs with 부랴부랴 ('frantically') and 밤새다 ('pull an all-nighter'). It carries a self-aware, procrastinator's tone — Koreans say 발등에 불 떨어져야 움직인다 ('I only move once the fire hits my foot') about their own last-minute habit. Register is casual-to-polite and it is everywhere around work and deadlines. The English-speaker pitfall: do not read it literally as a burn injury, and remember 떨어지다 here means 'falls/drops,' not 'runs out' — so 'the fire fell' = the crisis has arrived, not departed.

mistakes: Don't read it literally as a burn injury — it is about sudden urgency, not pain, so 'My foot got burned' is a complete mis-hearing.
It's 발등 (the top/instep of the foot), not 발 ('foot') — drop 등 and the vivid image of an ember landing on the exposed instep is lost.
Keep 떨어지다 in the right direction: it means the fire FELL (the crisis is here), so don't confuse it with the meaning 'to run out / be used up.'

english: to be right around the corner / extremely close in time or distance (lit. 'it's right in front of your nose')
usage: 시험이 코앞이야, 큰일 났어.
The exam is right around the corner — I'm in trouble.
Casual; time sense, looming pressure
마감이 코앞이라 정신없어요.
The deadline's right on top of us, so it's hectic.
Polite; -이라 = 'since it is'; very common with 마감
편의점 코앞인데 귀찮아서 안 나가.
The convenience store is right there but I'm too lazy to go.
Distance sense — 'a stone's throw'
코앞에 두고도 못 찾았어.
It was right under my nose and I still couldn't find it.
코앞에 두다 = 'to have right in front of you'
examples: 이사 날짜가 코앞이라 짐 싸느라 바빠요.
Moving day is almost here, so I'm busy packing.
-느라 = 'busy doing'; imminent event (time)
설날이 코앞인데 기차표를 아직 못 구했어.
Lunar New Year is around the corner and I still can't get a train ticket.
Seasonal urgency; 구하다 = 'to secure/get'
회사가 집 코앞이라 걸어서 5분이면 가요.
The office is right by my place — five minutes on foot.
Real-situation distance: X 코앞 = 'right by X'
nuance: Literally 'right in front of the nose,' 코앞 (코 'nose' + 앞 'front') frames something as extremely near — either in TIME (an event/deadline almost upon you) or in DISTANCE (a place a few steps away). The dividing line from the near-synonym 가깝다 ('to be close/near') is vividness and immediacy: 가깝다 is the neutral, measurable word ('the station is near'), while 코앞이다 dramatizes 'practically touching your face,' so it feels more pressing for time and more 'right there, no excuse' for distance. With time it loads on pressure (no buffer left); with distance it stresses how convenient/short the hop is. Register is casual-to-polite and it is used constantly. The English-speaker pitfall: 'right under my nose' in English usually means 'overlooked something obvious,' but Korean 코앞 plainly means 'very near' — so don't import the 'missed the obvious' nuance unless context (e.g. 코앞에 두고도 못 찾다) supplies it. Also write it as one word: 코앞, not 코 앞.

코앞 = 코 ('nose') + 앞 ('front'), i.e. 'right in front of the nose.'

mistakes: Write 코앞 as one word, not 코 앞 — it's a fixed compound noun.
Context decides whether it means 'soon' (time) or 'nearby' (distance); don't assume only the time reading, or you'll misread 집 코앞 ('right by the house').
Don't auto-map it to the English idiom 'right under my nose' (= 'missed something obvious'); plain 코앞이다 just means 'very close.'

english: to get chills down one's spine / be struck with fear or dread (lit. 'one's spine goes cold/shivery')
usage: 그 얘기 듣고 등골이 오싹했어.
I got chills down my spine hearing that.
Casual; fear/creepiness, past tense 오싹했어
밤에 혼자 그 길 걸으니까 등골이 오싹하더라고요.
Walking that road alone at night gave me the shivers.
Polite; -더라고요 reports a felt experience
사고 영상 보니까 등골이 다 오싹해.
Watching the accident footage sent a total chill down my spine.
다 here = 'completely,' intensifying the shiver
생각만 해도 등골이 서늘해.
Just thinking about it sends a chill down my back.
등골이 서늘하다 = close variant ('spine goes cool')
examples: 공포 영화에서 갑자기 소리가 나서 등골이 오싹했어요.
A sudden sound in the horror movie sent chills down my spine.
Horror/startle context
하마터면 큰일 날 뻔했다고 생각하니 등골이 오싹해.
Thinking I almost got into real trouble gives me the chills.
하마터면 ~ㄹ 뻔하다 = 'almost (nearly) happened'; dread over a close call
그 사람 눈빛이 너무 차가워서 등골이 오싹했어요.
His gaze was so cold it sent a shiver down my spine.
Real-situation: an unsettling person, not weather
nuance: 등골 is the line/marrow of the spine and 오싹하다 is that sudden, involuntary cold-shudder, so together they capture chills running down your back from fear, dread, eeriness, or the jolt of realizing you barely dodged disaster. The near-synonym is the listed variant 등골이 서늘하다 ('spine goes cool'): 서늘하다 is a touch quieter and more lingering-dread, while 오싹하다 is the sharper, sudden goose-bump spike — useful when a noise or revelation hits you all at once. Contrast it with plain 무섭다 ('to be scared'), which only names the emotion; 등골이 오싹하다 gives you the bodily sensation, which is why it shines in horror, ghost stories, and near-miss anecdotes. Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfall: this is fear-chills, NOT being physically cold from the weather (use 춥다 for that), and you must keep the body-part partner — 등골 goes with 오싹하다/서늘하다, so don't graft on 춥다 ('등골이 춥다' is unnatural).

Don't replace it with bare 무섭다 ('scary') when you mean the physical shiver — 무섭다 names the feeling, 등골이 오싹하다 conveys the spine reaction.

english: to praise someone lavishly / can't stop praising (lit. 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — from talking so much)
usage: 엄마가 너 칭찬을 입에 침이 마르게 하더라.
Mom couldn't stop singing your praises.
Casual; usual frame 입에 침이 마르게 + 칭찬하다
사장님이 그 직원을 입에 침이 마르도록 칭찬하셨어요.
The boss praised that employee to no end.
Polite; 마르도록 ('to the point of drying') is the common form
다들 그 식당을 입에 침이 마르게 추천해.
Everyone recommends that restaurant nonstop.
Extends to enthusiastic recommendations (추천하다)
입에 침이 마르게 자랑하던데 진짜 좋은가 봐.
They bragged about it endlessly, so it must be really good.
With 자랑하다 = relentless bragging
examples: 선생님이 네 그림을 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하셨어.
The teacher praised your drawing to the skies.
Lavish praise; -게 turns it adverbial
친구가 그 카페를 입에 침이 마르도록 얘기해서 가 봤어요.
My friend raved about that cafe so much that I went.
Praise leading to action; -아서 ('so') links cause to result
할머니는 손주 얘기만 나오면 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하세요.
Grandma gushes nonstop whenever her grandkids come up.
Real-situation habitual gushing; -세요 honorific for grandma
nuance: Literally 'the saliva in one's mouth dries up' — talk up how wonderful someone or something is for long enough and your mouth runs dry, so it means to praise lavishly, tirelessly, without pause. The dividing line from plain 칭찬하다 ('to praise') is intensity and duration: 칭찬하다 can be a single 'good job,' whereas 입에 침이 마르게 칭찬하다 means going on and on, gushing. It almost never stands alone — it is an adverbial that clamps onto a verb, nearly always 칭찬하다 ('praise'), 자랑하다 ('brag'), or 추천하다 ('recommend'), in the set forms 입에 침이 마르게 or 입에 침이 마르도록. The tone is warm and admiring. Casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfall: it has nothing to do with literal thirst or a dry mouth from dehydration, and you must not drop the partner verb — saying just '입에 침이 마르다' to mean 'I'm thirsty' is wrong; thirst is 목이 마르다 ('throat is dry').

mistakes: It means praising endlessly, not literally being thirsty or having a dry mouth — for real thirst use 목이 마르다 ('my throat is dry').
Don't drop the verb — it's used as 입에 침이 마르게/마르도록 + (칭찬하다/자랑하다/추천하다), not as a standalone statement.
Don't conjugate it as a finished action ('입에 침이 말랐다' to describe one compliment); it lives in the adverbial -게/-도록 form modifying the praising verb.

english: to work well together / be in sync as a team (lit. 'one's hands and feet match')
usage: 우리 둘은 손발이 잘 맞아.
The two of us work together really well.
Casual; 잘 ('well') is the usual partner adverb
새 팀이랑 손발이 맞아서 일이 수월해요.
I'm in sync with the new team, so work goes smoothly.
Polite; ~이랑 손발이 맞다 = 'in sync WITH ~'
손발이 안 맞아서 자꾸 실수가 나.
We're out of sync, so mistakes keep happening.
손발이 안 맞다 = the opposite
오래 같이 일하니까 손발이 척척 맞네.
We've worked together so long we're perfectly in sync.
척척 = 'smoothly, snappily,' an intensifying mimetic
examples: 주방이랑 홀이 손발이 맞아야 장사가 잘돼요.
The kitchen and the floor have to be in sync for business to run well.
Restaurant teamwork; -아야 = 'only if'
둘이 손발이 맞아서 행사를 무사히 끝냈어.
The two were in sync and pulled off the event without a hitch.
무사히 = 'safely, without incident'
처음엔 손발이 안 맞았는데 이제 호흡이 잘 맞아요.
At first we were out of sync, but now we work in great harmony.
Real-situation: 호흡이 맞다 is a close synonym
nuance: Literally 'hands and feet match,' it describes two or more people whose actions line up like a well-rehearsed team — the right rhythm of cooperation where each anticipates the other. The dividing line from the near-synonym 호흡이 맞다 ('breathing matches') is subtle: both mean 'in sync,' but 손발이 맞다 leans toward coordinated physical/operational action (who does what, timing of tasks), while 호흡이 맞다 leans toward an intuitive feel and shared tempo, common in performance or sport. Crucially, this is about working chemistry, NOT affection — it is not friendship or romance. The opposite 손발이 안 맞다 means people keep tripping over each other. Register is casual-to-polite, ubiquitous at work and on any team. The English-speaker pitfall: 'we match' tempts learners to use it for personality or romantic compatibility, but that is 잘 어울리다 / 궁합이 맞다; and because it is inherently mutual, you cannot be 손발이 맞다 with yourself — it always needs two-plus parties, marked with ~와/과 or ~이랑.

Don't confuse it with 호흡이 맞다 carelessly: 손발 stresses coordinated actions/tasks, 호흡 stresses intuitive shared rhythm.

english: to actively step up and help / throw oneself into something wholeheartedly (lit. 'to take off one's shoes and step forward')
usage: 네가 발 벗고 나서 줘서 진짜 고마워.
Thank you for stepping up and really pitching in.
Casual; -아 주다 ('do it for me') adds the favor nuance
이웃들이 발 벗고 나서서 도와줬어요.
The neighbors went out of their way to help.
Polite; -아서 chains 'stepped up AND helped'
회사가 발 벗고 나서서 문제를 해결했어.
The company actively stepped in and solved the problem.
Subject can be an organization taking initiative
친구 일이라면 발 벗고 나서는 사람이야.
He's the type to drop everything to help a friend.
~라면 ('when it comes to ~'); describes a generous character
examples: 선배가 발 벗고 나서서 취업을 도와줬어요.
A senior went all in to help me find a job.
Going above and beyond for someone
다들 발 벗고 나서서 이사를 도와줘서 금방 끝났어.
Everyone pitched in wholeheartedly with the move, so it finished fast.
Group effort; 금방 = 'in no time'
그 문제는 아무도 발 벗고 나서지 않아서 오래 방치됐어요.
Nobody stepped up for that issue, so it was left alone for ages.
Real-situation negative — no one took initiative; 방치되다 = 'be left neglected'
nuance: Literally 'to take off your shoes and step forward' — in old Korea shoes were valuable, so kicking them off to wade barefoot into a muddy job signalled 'I'm all in, no holding back,' hence eagerly stepping up to help, not half-heartedly. The dividing line from plain 돕다 ('to help') is the volunteered, wholehearted energy: 돕다 can be passive or asked-for, but 발 벗고 나서다 praises someone for taking the initiative for others, going out of their way. Compare 앞장서다 ('to take the lead / go in front'), which stresses leading a group from the front, while 발 벗고 나서다 stresses self-sacrificing willingness regardless of rank. It is warm and approving — almost always a compliment. Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: watch the spacing, 발 벗고 나서다 is three orthographic words (not 발벗고); and because it implies voluntary, eager involvement, don't use it for reluctant, grudging, or coerced help.

english: to feel the weight of responsibility / feel heavily burdened (lit. 'one's shoulders are heavy')
usage: 책임이 커서 어깨가 무거워.
The responsibility is big, so I feel the weight of it.
Casual; 책임 ('responsibility') is the core partner noun
중요한 일을 맡아서 어깨가 무겁습니다.
I've taken on an important task, so I feel the responsibility.
Polite/formal -습니다; staple of work speeches
가장으로서 어깨가 무거워요.
As the breadwinner, I carry a heavy load.
~로서 ('in the role of'); family responsibility
기대가 큰 만큼 어깨가 더 무거워.
The bigger the expectations, the heavier the burden.
~만큼 ('to the extent that') links expectation to pressure
examples: 팀장이 되니까 어깨가 무거워졌어요.
Becoming team lead made the responsibility feel heavier.
New role; -아지다 = 'became'
다들 나만 믿는다고 하니까 어깨가 무거워.
Everyone says they're counting on me, so I feel the weight.
Pressure from others' trust
큰 프로젝트를 혼자 맡아서 어깨가 너무 무거워요.
I'm handling a big project alone, so the burden feels heavy.
Real-situation heavy workload; 혼자 = 'alone'
nuance: Literally 'heavy shoulders,' it expresses the psychological weight of responsibility or others' expectations pressing down on you — the felt seriousness of a duty. The dividing line from the near-synonym 부담스럽다 ('to feel burdened/pressured') is tone and dignity: 부담스럽다 can be mild, even social (a gift is 부담스럽다 because it's too much), and is more neutrally about discomfort, whereas 어깨가 무겁다 is a humble, slightly noble admission that an important charge rests on you — which is why it is the go-to line in acceptance speeches, new-role announcements, and earnest talk about duty. Habitual partners: 책임 ('responsibility'), 기대 ('expectation'), 맡다 ('to take on'). Register runs casual all the way to formal. The relief counterpart is 어깨가 가벼워지다 ('shoulders get lighter'). The English-speaker pitfalls: this is emotional/responsibility weight, NOT literal sore or stiff shoulders (that's 어깨가 결리다/아프다), and don't confuse it with 어깨가 처지다 ('shoulders droop'), which means feeling discouraged or dejected, a different emotion.

english: to be shameless / thick-skinned / have a lot of nerve (lit. 'one's face is thick')
usage: 걔 진짜 얼굴 두껍다, 또 부탁하네.
He's got some nerve — asking for a favor again.
Casual, mildly critical; 을/를 often dropped: 얼굴 두껍다
그런 부탁을 하다니 얼굴이 두꺼우시네요.
Asking for that takes a lot of nerve.
Polite but pointed; -시- here is sarcastically deferential
나도 좀 얼굴 두꺼워져야 하나 봐.
Maybe I need to grow a thicker skin.
Self-talk; -아지다 = 'become'; positive 'less self-conscious' sense
낯짝이 두꺼워서 미안한 줄을 몰라.
He's so brazen he doesn't even feel sorry.
낯짝/낯이 두껍다 = blunter, harsher variants
examples: 얼굴이 두꺼워서 거절을 당해도 또 시도해요.
He's thick-skinned, so even after a no he tries again.
Persistence read as shamelessness
그렇게 민폐 끼치고도 태연한 거 보면 얼굴 두껍다.
Causing all that trouble and staying calm — what nerve.
민폐(를) 끼치다 = 'to be a nuisance'
면접 땐 얼굴이 좀 두꺼워야 떨지 않아요.
For interviews you need a bit of thick skin so you don't get nervous.
Real-situation: mildly positive 'don't be shy' sense
nuance: Literally 'thick face,' it labels someone shameless or brazen — a person who feels no embarrassment where they should. English actually shares the image in 'thick-skinned,' but beware: English 'thick-skinned' is usually a compliment ('unbothered by criticism'), whereas Korean 얼굴이 두껍다 is most often mildly negative or teasing ('no shame'). It can flip positive only in contexts like interviews or public speaking, meaning 'not easily flustered.' The dividing line from the near-synonym 뻔뻔하다 ('to be brazen/impudent') is bluntness: 뻔뻔하다 is the plain adjective and can sound flatly accusatory, while 얼굴이 두껍다 is the idiomatic, often lighter or jokier phrasing. Blunter, rougher variants are 낯이 두껍다 and 낯짝이 두껍다, and the noun for the trait is 철면피 ('iron face'). Register is casual-to-polite. The pitfalls: it has nothing to do with literal skin thickness, and tone-watch — it can land as an insult, so don't aim it bluntly at someone you must keep polite footing with.

english: to be incredibly busy / have no time to even breathe (lit. 'no moment to even open one's eyes and nose')
usage: 요즘 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠.
I'm so swamped these days I can't even catch a breath.
Casual; almost always with 바쁘다, joined by -이 (눈코 뜰 새 없이)
연말이라 눈코 뜰 새 없이 지내고 있어요.
It's year-end, so I'm run off my feet.
Polite; -고 있다 ('have been') for an ongoing hectic stretch
애 둘 키우느라 눈코 뜰 새가 없어.
Raising two kids leaves me no time to breathe.
새가 없다 form with subject 이/가
오픈 시간엔 눈코 뜰 새 없이 손님이 밀려와.
At opening time customers pour in nonstop.
밀려오다 = 'to flood in'; workplace rush
examples: 이사하고 정리하느라 눈코 뜰 새 없었어요.
I was swamped moving and unpacking.
-느라 ('busy with') + past; a big one-off task
행사 준비로 일주일 내내 눈코 뜰 새 없이 일했어.
I worked flat out all week preparing for the event.
일주일 내내 = 'all week long'; sustained busy period
식당이 점심엔 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바빠서 정신이 하나도 없어요.
The restaurant is so slammed at lunch I can't think straight.
Real-situation: 정신이 없다 ('frazzled') stacks naturally
nuance: Literally 'no gap (새 = 사이, 'interval') to even open your eyes and nose,' it is a vivid hyperbole for being so frantically busy you can't spare a single second. The dividing line from plain 바쁘다 ('to be busy') is sheer intensity: 바쁘다 covers any level of busy, while 눈코 뜰 새 없다 is the extreme top end — you can't even blink. It functions almost entirely as an adverbial intensifier in the set frame 눈코 뜰 새 없이 + 바쁘다/일하다/지내다, which is why textbooks treat 눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁘다 as one chunk. Note 새 here is the noun 사이/간격 ('gap, interval'), not 새 ('bird') — that homophone trips beginners. Register is casual-to-polite, extremely common for a hectic patch at work or home. The English-speaker pitfalls: keep the spacing 눈코 뜰 새 없다 (눈코 is one word, 뜰 새 = 'a moment to open'), and don't deploy it for a calm, neutral 'I have no time' — there must be genuine, breathless busyness for it to fit.

english: to get ripped off / be overcharged (lit. 'to wear a gourd dipper')
usage: 관광지에서 완전 바가지 썼어.
I got totally ripped off at the tourist spot.
Casual; 를 often dropped (바가지 쓰다); buyer overpays
택시 타다가 바가지 쓴 것 같아요.
I think I got overcharged in the taxi.
Polite; -ㄴ 것 같다 ('seems that') softens a suspicion
여기 비싸니까 바가지 쓰지 않게 가격 먼저 물어봐.
It's pricey here, so ask the price first to avoid getting fleeced.
-지 않게 ('so as not to'); practical advice
사장이 외국인한테 바가지를 씌웠어.
The owner ripped the foreigner off.
바가지(를) 씌우다 = the SELLER does the overcharging
examples: 축제 음식이 평소의 두 배라 바가지 쓴 기분이었어요.
The festival food was double the usual price — felt like a ripoff.
Inflated event pricing; 평소의 두 배 = 'double the usual'
시세 모르고 샀다가 바가지 썼어.
I bought it without knowing the going rate and got overcharged.
시세 = 'market/going price'; -다가 marks the slip-up
흥정 안 하면 시장에서 바가지 쓰기 쉬워요.
If you don't haggle you can easily get fleeced at the market.
Real-situation: 흥정 ('haggling') pairs naturally
nuance: Literally 'to wear a gourd dipper (바가지),' it means to be charged far more than something is worth — to get ripped off. The image is folk: traditionally one was said to overpay a debt 'as if a gourd of charges were dumped on your head.' It thrives in talk of tourist traps, taxis, markets, and festivals. The dividing line from plain 비싸다 ('to be expensive') is fairness: 비싸다 just means the price is high (possibly justified), whereas 바가지(를) 쓰다 implies you were unfairly gouged above the fair rate. The crucial grammar pair: 바가지(를) 쓰다 = YOU, the buyer, overpaid (쓰다 'to wear/put on'), while 바가지(를) 씌우다 = the SELLER puts the gouge on someone else (씌우다, the causative 'to make wear'). It is often shortened to just 바가지. Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: don't reverse 쓰다 ('got ripped off') and 씌우다 ('ripped someone off'), and don't use it for poor product quality — that's 별로다 or 안 좋다; 바가지 is strictly about being overcharged.

english: you won't get anything out of it / there'll be nothing in it for you (often a warning or threat) (lit. 'there's not even broth')
usage: 한 번만 더 늦으면 국물도 없어.
Be late one more time and you'll get nothing from me.
Casual warning/threat; -으면 ('if') sets the condition
약속 안 지키면 국물도 없을 줄 알아.
If you break the promise, don't expect anything good.
Half-joking threat; -을 줄 알아 = 'you'd better know / be warned'
이번에 도와줘도 나한테 국물도 없더라.
Even though I helped this time, I got nothing out of it.
-아도 ('even if'); complaining about zero payoff
그렇게 해 봤자 너한테 국물도 없어.
Even if you do that, there's nothing in it for you.
-아 봤자 ('no matter how much you ~'); a pointless effort
examples: 사장님이 또 실수하면 국물도 없다고 하셨어요.
The boss said if it happens again there'll be no mercy.
Workplace warning relayed with -다고 하다
내 말 안 들으면 다음부턴 국물도 없을 거야.
If you don't listen to me, next time you'll get nothing.
Parent/older-sibling tone; 다음부터 = 'from next time'
밤새 도왔는데 고맙단 말도 없고, 정말 국물도 없네.
I helped all night and didn't even get a thanks — nothing to show for it.
Real-situation: no reward at all, resigned -네 ending
nuance: Literally 'there isn't even broth (국물),' the image is a shared pot scraped so clean that not a drop of soup is left for you — so it means there is nothing to be gained: no benefit, no leftover, no mercy. Its dominant use is a half-joking warning or threat from someone with the upper hand: '한 번만 더 그러면 국물도 없어' ('do that once more and you'll get nothing from me'). A second use is grumbling that an effort yielded zero reward ('도와줘도 국물도 없더라'). The dividing line from a plainer warning like 가만 안 둬 ('I won't let it slide') is flavor: 가만 안 두다 threatens active punishment, whereas 국물도 없다 threatens withholding any goodwill or payoff — the carrot vanishes rather than a stick appearing. Register is firmly casual and the threat reading is blunt, so it suits friends, family, or clearly informal settings. The English-speaker pitfall: 국물 here is NOT literal soup — it's figurative 'leftover benefit/share,' so don't picture food; and because the tone is so informal and can sting, never deploy it in polite or professional speech where you must stay deferential.

english: to throw cold water on something / ruin the mood or kill the momentum (lit. 'to pour cold water over')
usage: 분위기 좋았는데 걔가 찬물을 끼얹었어.
The mood was great but he threw cold water on it.
Casual; 분위기 ('mood/vibe') is the classic object being ruined
좋은 소식에 찬물을 끼얹고 싶진 않지만요.
I don't mean to rain on the good news, but…
Polite hedge before delivering bad news
다들 신났는데 그 말 한마디가 찬물을 끼얹었어요.
Everyone was excited, but that one comment killed it.
말 한마디 = 'a single remark' as the subject
계획에 자꾸 찬물 끼얹지 말고 좀 응원해 줘.
Stop pouring cold water on the plan and cheer me on.
-지 말다 ('don't'); 을 dropped colloquially
examples: 회의 분위기가 살아나려는데 부장님이 찬물을 끼얹었어요.
The meeting was warming up, but the manager threw cold water on it.
-려는데 = 'just as it was about to'; workplace momentum killed
다 같이 여행 가자던 분위기에 한 명이 찬물을 끼얹었어.
Someone threw cold water on the whole let's-go-on-a-trip vibe.
Group plans deflated by one person
축하 자리에 굳이 찬물을 끼얹는 말을 할 필요는 없잖아.
There's no need to say something that ruins a celebration.
Real-situation: 굳이 ('needlessly') advising tact
nuance: Literally 'to pour cold water over (something hot),' it means to suddenly kill an upbeat mood, excitement, or building momentum — typically with a negative comment or unwelcome news — like dousing a warm fire. The dividing line from the near-synonym 김(을) 빼다 / 김새다 ('to let the steam out / deflate') is agency: 김새다 often just happens (the excitement fizzles on its own), whereas 찬물을 끼얹다 frames an active, deliberate party who throws the buzzkill. It presupposes there WAS heat — enthusiasm, a rising vibe, a plan everyone was hyped about — so it needs momentum to ruin. Habitual partners: 분위기에 ('to the mood'), 좋은 소식에 ('to good news'), 계획에 ('to a plan'). Register is casual-to-polite. The English-speaker pitfalls: spelling — it's 끼얹다 (kki-eon-da), an easy verb to mangle (the 받침 ㄶ in 얹 → pronounced 언), not 끼언다 or 끼엊다; and don't apply it to just any bad news — there must be a positive mood or built-up excitement present for the 'cold water' image to land.
